extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for interpreting patent claims and special claim language, plus principles governing the nature and transfer (assignment, grant, license) of patent rights and the patent monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of foreign words in patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign words occurring in a patent are to be interpreted by the context and the real object of the inventor, and to receive such meaning as will effect his intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply context and inventor's intent to give the foreign word the meaning that effectuates the invention. (Text cites White v. Allen (1868) and other authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'substantially as described' in a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'substantially as described' in the Claim signifies much or little, as the patentee evidently designed, and is always supposed to be incorporated in the Claim whether or not actually inserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrase relates only to the material features of the invention as shown by its purpose and the elements composing it; it allows the claim to be construed by reference to the specification for what the patentee intended to cover. (Cites Matthews v. Schonebeiger and others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'as herein described' and reference to specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The similar phrase 'as herein described' likewise refers to the specification for a fuller and more exact statement of the subject-matter of the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such phrases appear, interpret the claim in light of the specification; the specification may supply elements not explicitly mentioned in the claim. (Cites Seymour v. Osborne.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of the word 'specification' depends on context
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'specification' is sometimes employed to denote both the Claim and the Description, and sometimes only the Description; when used without 'claim' it may mean the entire paper (Description and Claims), but when 'claim' is also used it often means the Description only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether 'specification' denotes Description+Claims or Description alone by context and statutory references. (Cites Wilson v. Coon and statutory sections.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims referring to the specification must be construed by it
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims which refer to the specification must be construed by the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim points to the specification (e.g., via phrases like 'as described'), the specification governs construction and may make a claim valid even if it appears on its face to cover only a function or result. (Cites Gottfried v. Philip Best Brewing Co., Seymour v. Osborne.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation by words 'all as shown and described' in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The words in the Claim 'all as shown and described' limit the Claim to the exact thing shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such limiting language may confine the claim to the precise form depicted in the drawings and description. (Cites Osceola Mfg. Co. v. Pie.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate claims cannot be construed together as one
rubrics_metrics.description: Two apparently separate Claims cannot be construed together as one Claim and be supported by each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merge separate claims to create a single claim scope; each claim must stand on its own. (Cites Seymour v. McCormick.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two patents cannot be construed to supplement each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Two patents cannot be construed to supplement each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid interpreting one patent in light of another to fill gaps; each patent's disclosure must be self-sufficient for claim construction. (Cites Budes v. Rand, McNally & Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of terms admitting degrees (e.g., 'tight','hard','hot')
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms admitting of degrees — such as 'tight,' 'hard,' 'hot,' and the like — refer to that degree which is best suited to the purposes of the invention as indicated by its practical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree in light of the invention's practical use and what the skilled artisan would consider suitable; examples: 'to be hardened' means made as hard as possible; 'free from defect' means sufficiently free for practical purposes. (Cites Robinson v. Sutter, Monce v. Adams, Adams v. Bridgewater Iron Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase 'in any other convenient manner' construed broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'in any other convenient manner' includes every method which the invention can perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret this phrase to cover modes of operation the device can practically perform, not just the specific methods shown. (Cites Illinois Central R.R. Co. v. Turrill.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'suitable materials'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'suitable materials' embraces all known materials proper for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow reasonable substitutions of materials known in the art for the stated purpose. (Cites Bailey Washing & Wringing Mach. Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'making/selling' and 'use' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'making' or 'selling' of a substance is essentially distinct from its 'use', and a patent for the latter does not confer upon the patentee any exclusive right to the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent claiming only the use of an item does not give rights to make or sell it; drafting and claim analysis must keep these distinctions clear. (Cites Keystone Bridge Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of special words by persons skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Other special words are interpreted in view of the practical character of the invention and as they would ordinarily be employed by persons skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ordinary meaning in the relevant art and practical considerations; courts will interpret terms as a skilled artisan would. (General guidance from treatise.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic vs specific: 'generic' is a relative term
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'generic' is relative in its application: the same invention may be generic as to some inventions and specific as to others; interpret according to the nature of the operation or instrument and its position in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a term is generic or specific by reference to the technology and the state of the art; examples and authorities provided in the text (e.g., Sx parta Ewart).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'manufacture' can vary
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'manufacture' may denote the article made, or the means by which it is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'manufacture' contextually — it can mean either the product or the process depending on usage. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive treatment of descriptive phrases such as 'in the manner and for the purposes herein specified'
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Claim the words 'in the manner and for the purposes herein specified' should not be construed to cover every part shown in the drawings and Description, nor to confine the invention to the precise form therein shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These words should be read to avoid unduly narrow or overly broad interpretations: they do not automatically incorporate every drawing detail nor lock the patentee into a precise depicted form. (Cites Reed v. Chase.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specification to supply elements not in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'as herein described' or references to the specification may embrace elements not mentioned in the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the claim refers to the specification, courts may read in material features from the description to clarify the claim scope. (Cites Vance v. Campbell and others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific-word interpretation examples (judicial glosses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words have been judicially glossed: 'jointly' may mean 'by united action' not necessarily simultaneously; 'perfect' means perfect according to the standard required in the art; 'free from defect' means sufficiently free for practical purposes; 'concavo-convex' denotes degrees as mechanical judgment may show; 'or other part' can mean 'or other equivalent part'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case examples provided to guide how specific adjectives and compound descriptors are given practical, art-focused meanings rather than abstract literal meanings. (Cites Gold & Stock Telegraph Co.; Adams v. Bridgewater Iron Co.; Temple Pump Co. v. Goss Pump & Rubber Bucket Mfg. Co.; Babcock & Wilcox Co. v. Pioneer Iron Works.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patented invention consists of two distinct property elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Property in a patented invention is twofold: (1) property in the invention itself (the right to practice it — make, use, sell), and (2) property in the patent monopoly (the right to exclude others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are distinct in origin and nature: the inventive property arises from the inventive act and exists even without a patent; the monopoly arises from the statutory grant and is prohibitory in character and presupposes the invention. The monopoly is void if the inventive element does not exist. (Detailed exposition in §753.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alienability of the invention (rights to make/use/sell)
rubrics_metrics.description: The alienation of the invention, or the rights to make, use, or sell, is unrestricted by the nature of the property or the rules of law; these rights may be conferred separately or together and can be transferred before or after patent grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers of these subordinate rights do not, by themselves, transfer the patent monopoly; the transferee may exercise rights conferred without reference to others, and such transfers take effect inter partes regardless of the patent's validity. (Cites Dorsey Revolving Harvester Rake Co. v. Bradley Mfg. Co.; Adams v. Burke.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly is indivisible except territorially and transfer-restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: The alienation of the monopoly created by the patent is restricted: the monopoly is indivisible in subject-matter (cannot be split among independent persons in the same locality) but is divisible as to territorial area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law forbids division of the prohibitory power among multiple independent owners in the same territory because it would create contradictory rights; the monopoly may be vested in different owners for different territories. (Cites Gayler v. Wilder and other cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: First-class transfers (assignment/grant) vs second-class transfers (license)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two classes of conveyances: (a) First class transfers operate on both the invention and the monopoly (assignments and grants). (b) Second class transfers transfer the invention but not the monopoly (licenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments/grants bestow the prohibitory power within the specified area enabling the transferee to prevent others and obtain redress; licenses transfer subordinate rights without transferring the monopoly except by estoppel. Statutes and courts recognize these distinctions and assign technical terms accordingly. (See §§756–760.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a transfer to be a first-class transfer affecting the monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: No transfer can be of the first class (i.e., transfer the monopoly) unless it conveys the entire interest, or an undivided portion of the entire interest, in the invention either for the whole United States or for some definite part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conveyances that leave the patentee any distinct and independent right in the invention are of the second class and cannot transfer the monopoly (except by estoppel). Assignments that convey exclusive rights to make, use, and sell for a defined territory effect a transfer of the monopoly for that territory. (Detailed in §§758–760.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial subdivision of monopoly and forms of conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: The first class of conveyances can be subdivided according to territorial limits: (i) conveyances transferring entire interest (or undivided portion) for the whole United States (Assignments), and (ii) conveyances transferring interest limited to a specified area (Grants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignment generally transfers the entire nationwide interest (or an undivided share thereof); a grant transfers monopoly rights limited to the described territory. The terms 'assignee' and 'grantee' are not synonymous. (Cites Gayler v. Wilder; statutory references.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of second-class transfers (licenses) on monopoly enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-class conveyances (licenses) transfer rights in the invention but not the monopoly; their sole operation upon the monopoly is that of an estoppel, preventing the transferor from enforcing prohibitory powers against the transferee to impair the transferred interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensee gains no authority to exclude others (no monopoly) unless the license's terms or later assignments imply such authority; the licensee may, in some cases, invoke the patentee's prohibitory powers in his favor, but the monopoly remains legally with the patentee. (See §757.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly passes with exclusive rights conferred for a territorial extent
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patentee bestows on any person the exclusive rights in the invention, or an undivided portion of the exclusive rights within a given area, the monopoly to the same territorial extent passes entirely to that person (or resides undivided in joint-owners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers conferring exclusive make/use/sell rights for a locality transfer the monopoly for that locality; co-ownership of an undivided portion results in joint ownership of the monopoly for that territorial scope. (Explained in §758.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment defined and its effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment is a transfer of the entire interest in a patented invention, or of an undivided portion of such entire interest, as to every section of the United States; it operates to transfer the monopoly where these conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments and the rights under them rest on statute and case law; an assignment that conveys the entire unqualified monopoly for the specified territory enables the assignee to sue and to exercise prohibitory powers. (Cites Potter v. Holland and statutory references.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality and substance: an assignment short of full monopoly is a license
rubrics_metrics.description: Any assignment that is short of conveying the entire and unqualified monopoly which the patentee held in the territory specified is, between the parties, a mere license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will treat transfers that purport to convey monopoly rights but do not transfer the entire interest (or an undivided part) as licenses; practical effect and wording determine whether transfer is an assignment or license. (Cites Littlefield v. Perry.)
